title: Rethinking doctoral assessment for a changing PhD
summary:

The post Rethinking doctoral assessment for a changing PhD appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Charlotte Fawcett, former HEPI intern and Pathways Outreach Assistant at De Montfort University.

For decades, PhD assessment has followed a broadly consistent model: candidates submit a written thesis before defending their research in an oral viva voce. Internal and external examiners use the viva to test the candidate’s understanding, establish ownership of the work and assess its original contribution to knowledge.

But as the PhD itself changes, an important question is becoming harder to ignore: does the traditional assessment model still adequately assess candidates, their work and their potential?

A model built around the monograph

The traditional PhD thesis is usually a monograph: a substantial, long-form work focused on a single subject and often written by a single author. This allows candidates to demonstrate sustained engagement with a research question and develop a coherent argument in depth.

However, the monograph may not be suitable for all types of PhD research. Increasingly, doctoral projects are collaborative: involving communities, organisations and industry partners, with contributions that extend beyond the written thesis. These ethical, social, community and policy contributions can be difficult to capture in an assessment model focused on individual research outputs.

This raises a broader question about what PhD assessment should recognise. If the purpose of a PhD is to demonstrate the ability to conduct rigorous, original research and contribute to knowledge, why should there be only one preferred way of demonstrating that achievement?

The viva: tradition under scrutiny

The viva is often presented as an essential and long-established feature of doctoral education. Its intellectual roots can be traced to traditions of oral disputation associated with Ancient Greece, where questioning and debate were used to test arguments.

There is a strong case for retaining this element of PhD assessment. The viva allows candidates to explain decisions that may not be apparent from the thesis, address weaknesses in their written work and demonstrate ownership of their research.

Yet tradition alone should not justify retaining a particular assessment method. In the UK, vivas are often conducted behind closed doors, raising questions about their transparency and validity. There are also concerns about whether the viva provides an equitable and reliable way of assessing candidates.

These concerns do not necessarily mean that the viva should be abolished. Instead, they demonstrate why one assessment format should not be treated as universally appropriate.

The problem with standardisation

The viva can be highly variable, with differences in questioning, examiner interactions and decision-making raising concerns about consistency. The format may also disadvantage some candidates, particularly those who experience anxiety or are neurodivergent. Vivas commonly last several hours and can involve significant costs, particularly when external examiners must travel.

It might be tempting to respond to these inconsistencies by making the viva more standardised. But this could solve one problem while creating another.

The diversity of doctoral research makes complete standardisation neither desirable nor necessarily possible. A two-hour oral examination may be appropriate for one candidate and discipline but poorly suited to another. A monograph may provide an excellent assessment of some research while being an inadequate representation of collaborative, creative, practice-based or community-engaged research.

The answer to inconsistency, therefore, should not necessarily be to make every PhD look the same. It should be to establish consistent expectations while allowing diverse forms of evidence.

Alternatives already exist

The traditional model can be adapted. Alternative thesis formats have long been used in disciplines such as music, drama and creative writing. Another established model is the journal or publication-based thesis. Candidates submit a series of peer-reviewed articles alongside introductory and concluding chapters that establish the coherence and contribution of the research.

These approaches demonstrate that doctoral assessment does not need to have a single format. They also highlight an important distinction – standardising the criteria for a doctorate is not the same as standardising the way those criteria are demonstrated.

A PhD should continue to meet robust expectations around originality, methodological rigour, critical thinking and contribution to knowledge. But candidates should have greater scope to demonstrate those qualities through outputs appropriate to their research.

From standardised processes to common standards

As the PhD continues to evolve, the range of outputs submitted for assessment is likely to expand.

Collaborative research may generate community resources, policy outputs or other forms of impact. Creative and practice-based research may require artefacts or performances. Digital research may generate datasets, software or other outputs that cannot be adequately represented through conventional means.

This does not mean that anything should count as a PhD. Greater diversity in assessment requires clearer principles, not weaker standards. Universities could establish a common framework defining what doctoral achievement means while giving candidates greater choice in how they demonstrate those achievements.

Reimagining doctoral assessment

There is an understandable institutional desire to standardise PhD assessment. Common processes can support quality assurance, consistency and comparability. But standardisation also has limits.

The PhD is, by nature, an individual research qualification. Research questions, methodologies, disciplines, outputs and collaborations vary enormously. A highly standardised assessment system risks producing consistency of process at the expense of validity of assessment.

We need common standards for what a doctorate represents, but greater diversity in how candidates demonstrate that they have achieved them.

This could mean broader recognition of different research outputs, greater consideration of collaborative and societal contributions, alternative approaches to the viva, and more flexibility for different disciplines and candidates.

The flaws in current PhD assessment should not lead us towards a more uniform system. They should prompt us to ask whether uniformity was ever the right goal. The future of doctoral assessment should be diverse by design, recognising the increasingly diverse ways in which PhD research creates knowledge and value.

title: McMahon Says ‘Institutional Decay’ Compelled a ‘Reckoning’
summary:
McMahon Says ‘Institutional Decay’ Compelled a ‘Reckoning’ jessica.blake@… Thu, 10/29/2026 - 03:00 AM In a speech Wednesday, the education secretary echoed what she said at Arizona State last week, this time praising Vanderbilt University as she focused on combating ideological bias and restoring public trust. Byline(s) Jessica Blake McMahon Says ‘Institutional Decay’ Compelled a ‘Reckoning’
jessica.blake@… Thu, 10/29/2026 - 03:00 AM

In a speech Wednesday, the education secretary echoed what she said at Arizona State last week, this time praising Vanderbilt University as she focused on combating ideological bias and restoring public trust.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
Education Secretary Linda McMahon declared President Donald Trump’s 2024 election “a turning point for higher education” during a speech at Vanderbilt University Wednesday, the fourth and final talk in her series entitled “The Next 250: American Education.”

“Violent riots erupted across campuses,” McMahon said, referring to the wave of pro-Palestinian student encampments that sprang up in the spring of 2024. But those protests, combined with dramatic declines in academic rigor, caught Americans’ attention, she said, and now, “a tide of reform is finally washing over our campuses—powered by some institutional leaders who have boldly acknowledged the need to rebuild public trust, restore sanity and revive a culture of excellence and accountability.”

“The most vivid examples of institutional decay rising to the surface compelled a reckoning,” she later said.

Two years later, with Trump in office, colleges and universities are returning to “the basic standards that powered centuries of academic vitality,” she said: protecting free speech and open inquiry, setting rigorous merit-based academic standards, and committing to putting Americans first.

Just as she did a week ago when she gave a similar speech on college affordability at Arizona State University, McMahon touted her host institution, Vanderbilt, for being a prime example of such renewal. She also pointed to Yale and Washington Universities, which, like Vanderbilt, have released reports acknowledging their role in politicizing academic research and eroding public trust in higher education.

She also praised the “more than 300 colleges” that have rolled back “discriminatory DEI mandates” and institutions including Ohio State, the University of Iowa and the University of North Carolina that have expanded or opened new civil discourse centers.

She effusively thanked Vanderbilt’s chancellor, Daniel Diermeier, for his leadership, calling the Nashville, Tenn., institution “a model of courage and clarity” that “lighted the way for the nation.”

“At a time when universities everywhere are being pushed, prodded and publicly pressured to issue statements on every social or geopolitical controversy, Vanderbilt refused to be swept along by the winds of the moment,” McMahon said.

Instead, it chose institutional neutrality.

And by “choosing this harder path, Vanderbilt is clearing the ground for the return of the pathbreaking research and intellectual vitality that make our campuses national treasures,” she said.

As she did in last week’s speech, McMahon started by inviting listeners to recall a time when higher education was at its best, “forging the ideas that would give birth to the American republic” and driving scientific innovation. Then she pivoted, drawing attention to the “stark” contrast between what once was and what students experience today. She accused many institutions of “succumbing to the idea that merit and excellence should be sacrificed to equity and ideology” and blamed federal grant makers who “fueled this campaign against intellectual rigor” by funding “intellectually hollow projects,” such as a Ph.D. dissertation that focused on “transgender Thai Buddhist artists.”

Finally, she turned her attention to how the Trump administration’s actions—particularly the seven “landmark” agreements it reached with institutions including Columbia and the University of Pennsylvania—are bringing “much‑needed scrutiny” to issues that went unaddressed for years.

McMahon did not mention her department’s proposed “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education,” which would have required institutions to make sweeping changes or risk losing federal funds—a move that spurred widespread condemnation. Nor did she mention the “Call to Action” letter she sent to colleges in August, which many experts describe as a significantly watered-down version of the compact.

The secretary noted that while Trump’s approach to this new era of higher ed has been cast as “heavy‑handed,” she’s surprised by how often she hears institutional leaders express “a quiet appreciation for the Trump administration’s approach” and how it “provides the air cover … to pursue the reforms they long knew were needed.”

McMahon did not say which institutional leaders have made such remarks.

She closed by urging institutions to promote the “good of the country.”

“They must reclaim the principles, the seriousness and the sense of mission that once made their institutions indispensable to the American project,” she said.

title: The Untapped Potential of Adult Learners
summary:
The Untapped Potential of Adult Learners Joshua.Bay Thu, 10/29/2026 - 03:00 AM New research identifies millions of California adults without college degrees and the institutional changes needed to help them enroll and graduate. Byline(s) Joshua Bay The Untapped Potential of Adult Learners
Joshua.Bay Thu, 10/29/2026 - 03:00 AM

New research identifies millions of California adults without college degrees and the institutional changes needed to help them enroll and graduate.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Nationwide, demand for workers with postsecondary credentials remains strong, even as demographic trends threaten to shrink the pipeline of prospective college students. In California, the number of high school graduates is projected to decline by more than 30 percent in the coming years, and college-going rates remain below previous levels.

At the same time, a college degree remains an important avenue to economic mobility for low- and middle-income families in the state, even as rising living costs put additional pressure on households. A new report from the research and policy organization California Competes argues that one potential solution to the state’s workforce and economic challenges lies in a population often overlooked by higher education: adults with a high school diploma but no college degree.

An estimated 6.4 million Californians ages 25 to 54 fall into this category, which the report refers to as “potential graduates.” Nearly half—48 percent, or roughly 3.1 million—have earned some college credits but not a degree, highlighting an opportunity for institutions to re-engage adults who have previously pursued higher education.

Su Jin Jez, chief executive officer of California Competes, said one of the biggest barriers to reaching these adults is that higher education remains largely structured around 18-year-old students with few responsibilities outside of college.

“Even the traditional 18-year-old in California is a lot different than they were 60 years ago,” Jez said, noting that the state’s higher education system has changed little since the Master Plan for Higher Education formalized its structure in 1960, despite significant shifts in the student population and economy over the past six decades.

“I would love for us to really think about who are the people in our state who should be in college, want to be in college and could be in college if we had a better structure for higher education,” she said.

The untapped population: The report notes that in the coming years, 46 percent of California jobs will require a college degree, raising concerns about whether the state will have enough college graduates to meet future workforce demands. Meanwhile, roughly 56 percent of the state’s working-age adults hold a college degree or other postsecondary credential, well below Gov. Gavin Newsom’s goal of 70 percent attainment by 2030.

Beyond identifying the size of California’s potential graduate population, the report examines their employment, family and financial circumstances to better understand the challenges they may face in pursuing a college degree.

Nearly three-quarters of potential graduates, or 74 percent, are employed, including 60 percent who work full-time, while 42 percent are parents of children under 18. Among those who are employed, three in 10 work in service or retail jobs, which often have unpredictable schedules.

Financial pressures create another potential barrier. Nearly half of the potential graduates, or 46 percent, live in households earning less than a living wage, defined in the report as the minimum income needed to cover basic necessities such as housing, food, transportation, health care and childcare, with estimates varying by household size and local living costs. Among potential graduates in single-adult households with children, fewer than a quarter earn a living wage.

Jez said the goal should be to ensure that students experience the benefits of higher education from the moment they enroll, rather than only after they complete a degree. That means connecting students with the state’s public assistance programs, such as CalFresh and CalWORKs, as well as providing access to quality childcare and safe, affordable housing.

“They see the value of higher education, but oftentimes that is not enough to actually get someone to take the step to enroll,” Jez said. “What we can do to make college more affordable for folks is to get people access to what they’re already eligible for.”

Geography shapes access to higher education, with about 40 percent of potential graduates living in California’s inland and more rural regions, where college options may be more limited.

The report also highlights the racial and ethnic diversity of the potential graduate population. Nearly half are Latino, predominantly of Mexican heritage, and most are people of color. Nearly half a million have limited English proficiency, underscoring the importance of integrating English-language instruction with college-level education and career avenues.

“There’s a racial justice issue and a real equity issue around income and the geographical diversity of our state,” Jez said. “Diversity is what makes California incredible, but it also means policymaking needs to be really targeted and intentional.”

Making college accessible: The report identifies institutional and policy changes that could help more adults enroll or return to college and complete a credential, including expanding online and hybrid instruction, awarding credit for prior learning, simplifying re-enrollment and credit transfer, removing Cal Grant barriers that exclude older students, and expanding affordable childcare for student parents.

Jez pointed to Shasta College and California State University, Sacramento, as examples of institutions working to better serve adult learners. Shasta College, for instance, offers an Accelerated College Education program that provides a structured, fast-track route for working adults to earn an associate degree or certificate.

For Jez, the findings underscore the need to rethink how higher education is structured and whom institutions are designed to serve.

“If you missed a moment when you’re at 18—or at 22 even—it shouldn’t be that you are now resigned to not be able to contribute to the state in the way that you most meaningfully could or that you don’t have the economic stability that would give you the ability to thrive,” Jez said.

“Our state, our higher ed institutions, need to recognize that it’s not just about enrollment management and budget,” she added. “It really is about California continuing to be a leader in our country and our world, and there’s a real moral imperative … to meaningfully connect Californians to higher education.”

title: How colleges are helping students build social skills for the workforce
summary: Much of the debate over higher education today centers on cost, career prospects and whether a college degree can prepare students for a rapidly changing job market. But in an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, one of the oldest skills taught on college campuses may be more valuable than ever. Paul Solman reports for our higher education series, Rethinking College.
full_text:
Geoff Bennett:

Much of the debate over higher education today centers on cost, career prospects, and whether a college degree can prepare students for a rapidly changing job market.

But in an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, one of the oldest skills taught on college campuses may be more valuable than ever.

Paul Solman reports for the next installment in our higher education series, Rethinking College.

Paul Solman:

Isolated by COVID, bombarded by social media, screen-swamped in general, and headed for an all-bets-are-off job market, no wonder today's students feel, to use a lament from my college days, as if they're up a tree, that is, precariously perched.

Well, most of us remember from college learning to fend for ourselves by making friends outside the safe bubble of home and high school. But nowadays, with all the job pressure today's students face, is learning to socialize still as crucial?

Jill Barry:

I think, for me, it is one of the most important aspects, because when you're in college, you're meeting all these people of different backgrounds and you want to be able to use that knowledge once you graduate into a job.

Paul Solman:

Is it the single most important aspect of college, learning to live on your own, be with other people?

Kosi Chugbo-Junius:

Yes, I think it is like the single most important. I think whether you're an engineer, whether you're a science person, business, anything, that's the one thing I think all -- any job you're looking for, anything you want to do beyond here is going to have in common. You're going to have to work with people.

Paul Solman:

For better or worse.

Kosi Chugbo-Junius:

For better or worse.

(LAUGHTER)

Paul Solman:

We started this story last spring at Michigan universities, where the emphasis from the top was crystal clear, not so much socializing as reorienting college to get students jobs.

Brendan Kelly, President, Eastern Michigan University:

It's not about courses and credit hours anymore. And that's been our model for the last 100 years.

Paul Solman:

Eastern Michigan University President Brendan Kelly.

Brendan Kelly:

We have to understand that our business is rooted in the student, and then has to be connected to their participation in the economy after graduation.

Paul Solman:

Job readiness is equally top of mind for Michigan State President Kevin Guskiewicz.

Kevin Guskiewicz, President, Michigan State University:

We have got a ranking recently two years in a row as top 10 among all publics for employability. That's a metric that we're proud of and one that we advertise proudly.

Paul Solman:

But when we talk to students, they emphasize something different.

Reilly Coon, Michigan State Graduate Student:

I come from a rural community in Northern Wisconsin, and so going to college for me was the first exposure I'd had to new ideas, new people. It was the most diverse environment I was ever in.

Paul Solman:

Michigan State grad student Reilly Coon got her undergraduate degree at the University of Wisconsin.

Reilly Coon:

I'm sure three years from now I won't remember every single thing or every reading, but the skills gained from that are I think essential for going out into the world and have definitely made me a more holistic human being and just helped me develop as a person.

Itzel Segovia, Michigan State Alumna:

I came from Texas. And it's a very big Latino community, so when I came here, it was, like, very diverse.

Paul Solman:

We heard the same thing from new MSU Itzel Segovia.

Itzel Segovia:

So I met people from all different backgrounds, and I will catch myself, like, on a Tuesday morning eating pho because of the friend that I made, and she's from Vietnam. So I think that it's essential to create those relationships in college, because that's one thing that will go with you through life.

Paul Solman:

And we didn't just hear it in Michigan; 800 miles east at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, same story.

Kosi Chugbo-Junius:

I came here, I didn't know a single person.

Paul Solman:

Senior Kosi Chugbo-Junius.

Kosi Chugbo-Junius:

Everything I have here, every resource I lean on is someone that I had to form like a social connection with. Like, I rely on that every day.

Paul Solman:

Seniors Jill Barry and Ben Luu.

Jill Barry:

When you're in college, you kind of develop a sense of self and you become more yourself, and you know how to communicate with people, and you're more confident in who you are.

Paul Solman:

When you first came here, how freaked out were you about, say, meeting other kids or meeting girls?

Ben Luu, Student, University of Massachusetts Amherst: Oh, I would say it was intimidating. But, as you get along, it gets easier. Like, now I'm an R.A. on campus, so I live in with a bunch of kids, and so it kind of builds on you. Like, when -- if you were to ask me in freshman year if I were to ever be an R.A., like, I would have never even dreamt of it. But as...

Paul Solman:

Would you have talked to me when you were a freshman if I came to you at a table?

Ben Luu:

Probably not. I would probably run away or something. I was a very shy kid in high school.

Paul Solman:

Shy, isolated. So many higher ed students these days actually report feeling lonely.

Betsy Cracco, University of Massachusetts Amherst: We start to see the erosion of social skills because people are spending so much time in virtual world. So when they come to campus, it might be the first time they're really immersed in a community.

Paul Solman:

Betsy Cracco runs the student well-being initiative at UMass Amherst.

More of a challenge now than it was?

Betsy Cracco:

More of a challenge now than it was. We started looking at loneliness as an outcome measure. In 2023, about 54 percent of the students here and higher than that nationally reported being lonely. We were able to get that down to about 42 percent, which is lower than the national average.

Paul Solman:

But 42 percent, that's four out of 10 kids who are walking by here now.

Betsy Cracco:

Not wrong. After the pandemic, we saw scores in social anxiety really peak, and they have started to taper back down. Students are really craving opportunities to be in person with each other. They're looking for sort of structured and scaffolded opportunities. This is the playdate generation.

Paul Solman:

What does that mean?

Betsy Cracco:

For a lot of these young people, they were not told to go out and come back when the lights go -- turn back on, on the street, right, that, you know, when we were younger, perhaps go outside, and play and come back.

Paul Solman:

UMass has created what it calls scaffolding for students to interact with one another, often in phone- and screen-free ways, bonfires, climbing events, even a glow light dance party.

The goal, says Christopher Blakely, head of student engagement at UMass:

Christopher Blakely, University of Massachusetts Amherst: Our desire is that we design a campus where every student is known.

Paul Solman:

But there are 20,000 students here. How could you?

Christopher Blakely:

And that's a challenge for us. So our design is that every student is known. They're not known by everybody, but they're known by somebody, so that we build a student engagement model where it's reciprocal, that we're not asking students to engage just with us, but we're engaging with the students.

Paul Solman:

So in an era where getting a job is iffier than ever, schools like UMass and Michigan State and Eastern Michigan have been forced to realize that soft skills are required, both for a non-lonely offline life and for a shape-changing work force.

Laura Lee McIntyre, Provost, Michigan State University:

Campuses are a place where young people learn to become adults.

Paul Solman:

Michigan State University Provost Laura Lee McIntyre.

Laura Lee McIntyre:

Over a span of four years, they're managing their schedules. They're managing their social commitments. They're managing their appointments with their advisers and their faculty. They are managing their workload.

Paul Solman:

And the soft skills that may well, in the era of AI, be the work skills of the future.

Laura Lee McIntyre:

There's something unique about the conditions under which college campuses are intentional about student well-being in the classroom, but beyond. That preparation prepares our students, who are young adults, to transition into the world of work and life.

Paul Solman:

And so, yes, kids up a tree, but socializing.

For the "PBS News Hour," Paul Solman in Amherst, Massachusetts.

title: 5 expert takeaways on 2026 midterm election security
summary: With Election Day around the corner, states have been working hard to prepare, with some adopting new congressional maps and voting rules on top of normal election security measures. PBS News' Liz Landers and Votebeat editorial director Jessica Huseman hosted a Reddit "Ask Me Anything" Q&A on Wednesday to address people's questions.
full_text:
Several questions touched on people's concerns about their vote being tampered with or not being counted, alongside broader concerns about possible meddling from the federal government.

The Trump administration is attempting measures that haven't been tried before, Huseman said. Those actions include attempts to change election rules through executive orders, repeated demands for voter data and efforts to expand the government's role – specifically the executive branch – in elections. All of this amounts to an "unprecedented environment now," she said.

And yet, "elections officials are confident the system will hold," she added.

Here are five major takeaways from the Reddit AMA.

Evidence shows that illegal voting is extremely rare

Trump has routinely cast doubt on the security of the vote, making false claims of "rampant" voter fraud even a week ahead of Nov. 3.

The president, who has continued to falsely claim that the 2020 presidential election was "rigged," has fixated on rooting out what he claims is election fraud this election cycle. The Trump administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas to more than a dozen states requesting voter roll data, expanding its efforts to tamp down alleged noncitizen voting. But illegal voting by noncitizens voting is vanishingly rare.

READ MORE: Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say

Votebeat spent more than a year investigating claims from a group called the Election Truth Alliance that promoted a statistical analysis suggesting votes in the 2024 election had been manipulated in Pennsylvania, she said.

The nonprofit newsroom consulted nearly a dozen experts and put the Election Truth Alliance's claims through peer review.

"What we actually found was that the model would identify fraud even on datasets intentionally built not to contain any fraud," Huseman said. "Despite much of their analysis not standing up to scrutiny, it still managed to raise more than $400,000 in a single year."

WATCH: Inside Georgia's push to rebuild trust in elections after Trump's false claims

Huseman said it's worth remembering that "elections are not black boxes."

"In the places where the Election Truth Alliance alleged truly incredible problems, there were audits, observers, paper ballots and an entire staff of people whose jobs are ensuring the accuracy of these numbers," she said. "We can scrutinize the evidence as it's presented, but when we have it, we have to look it squarely in the face and call it what it is."

Trump can't declare a national emergency to interfere with elections

Nowhere in the U.S. Constitution does the president of the United States have express authority over how elections are run.

As laid out in the country's founding document, states determine the time, place and manner of elections. And Congress has a role in passing legislation over federal elections, though they have not passed major laws like this in a while, Landers said.

READ MORE: Immigrants seeking U.S. citizenship targeted in Trump administration's illegal voting crackdown

To put a finer point on it: The president cannot declare some kind of national emergency and expect all 50 states to stop their elections.

"I know from speaking with election officials across the country that they will not stop their election administration just because the president declared something over a process he does not have any legal authority," Landers said.

She also asked Trump in February if he would declare a national emergency — as some of his allies have urged. He said no at the time, adding he'd never heard about that.

Federal election monitors are there to observe

The Justice Department is planning to dispatch more than 1,000 federal election monitors to observe proceedings on Election Day. What they can do at polling places is fairly limited.

WATCH: DOJ monitoring plans and DHS voter checks raise concerns of election interference

To be clear: Federal election monitors are a normal part of both midterm and presidential elections, and the Biden administration deployed them in the 2024 presidential election cycle.

Watch the segment in the player above.

What is different this year is the number of federal election monitors that are being used, as well as the Trump administration's big public effort around it. A senior DOJ official told PBS News two weeks ago that they plan to send those 1,000-plus monitors to all 50 states.

WATCH: Examining the DOJ's effort to prosecute non-citizens accused of voting

These monitors must work within local and state laws and are only there to observe and take notes. If — and a big if — they see some kind of miscarriage of federal voting law, they are supposed to alert Main Justice headquarters in Washington, D.C., who will investigate after Election Day, Landers said.

In the last few months, PBS News has also heard from lawyers and voting experts about an increased presence of other kinds of observers at the polls, from across the spectrum.

One suggestion from a former career lawyer at the Justice Department is that if voters see anything at a polling location that seems weird or concerning to them, they should document what happened and share the information with a member of Congress, a local official, a voting rights organization or even speak with a news organization about it.

You can also ask your local election office if you can observe their work, Landers said. Many large and small jurisdictions, including Maricopa County in Arizona, and Paulding County in Georgia, have observation rooms or livestreams where the public can see how the business of elections is carried out.

A reminder about voter roll 'purges'

When it comes to states updating their voter rolls, including instances where eligible voters were kicked off the lists ahead of an election, Huseman noted that Votebeat is careful when using the word "purge" (like in "voter roll purge.")

This is because "list maintenance," or removing people from voter rolls is a "normal, necessary and actually enfranchising thing to do," she said, whereas "purge" suggests something bad happened.

WATCH: State voting officials join CISA security call with election 85 days away

"People die, move or otherwise become ineligible," she said. "Removing them from the rolls allows you to make sure they are on the right one, and voter registration outreach does not happen if someone appears to be registered even if they haven't lived in that place for years."

This is an important part of the process, she added. "When you see a headline saying that a state has removed 100,000 voters, that doesn't really tell you that much."

The questions instead should be: How many eligible voters were incorrectly removed, and did that actually prevent anyone from voting?

Huseman pointed to Votebeat's work with ProPublica and The Texas Tribune investigating Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's claim that the state had removed more than 6,500 noncitizens from the rolls. The outlets found the governor's claim misleading and identified U.S. citizens who'd been incorrectly flagged or removed from the state's list.

"That's a huge problem, but it's also important to distinguish between someone being flagged for investigation and actually losing their registration," Huseman said.

What have elections officials said about certifying the vote?

We received a handful of questions about election certification.

Landers pointed to the most prominent example involving election certification — or the refusal to do so — out of Otero County, New Mexico, where a county commissioner there refused to certify an election in June 2022 after questioning Dominion Voting Systems machines used in that election. The state Supreme Court forced the board to eventually certify the results.

This is a pretty cut-and-dry example of how the system works: If local election officials refuse to certify an election, it will be litigated by the candidates on the ballot and a judge will step in.

This also occurred in Cochise County, Arizona, in 2022, but the election was eventually certified there as well after a legal battle, even though the county did miss the state certification deadline.

This election cycle, Landers has spoken with a handful of local and state elections officials about the possible scenario of someone refusing to certify.

"No one I have talked with is worried that this will actually happen and stop the certification," she said. "Basically, there are checks and balances and deadlines for certification that campaigns are ready to sue over and state officials are ready to enforce."

title: As AI transforms global markets, Cyberport Venture & Capital Forum 2026 brings together the investors and innovators shaping what's next
summary:
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Global venture capital is surging in 2026, fuelled by concentrated investment in AI, digital infrastructure, robotics and other frontier technologies. At the same time, agentic AI, tokenisation, stable coins and programmable finance are accelerating the movement of capital across borders, giving rise to an emerging ‘agentic economy.’ 
Against this backdrop, CVCF 2026 aims to further energise and accelerate venture...
full_text:
Globally venture capital investment demonstrated strong momentum, reaching US$170.9 billion across 8,341 transactions in the third quarter of 2026 alone. According to Hendrick Sin, Chairman of the Cyberport Investors Network (CIN) Steering Group, AI-driven platforms continue to attract the lion’s share of investment.

Within the broader frontier technology landscape, enterprise AI and agentic AI have emerged as standout sectors.

This surge in private-market investment is matched by strong public markets. In the first nine months of 2026, Hong Kong’s IPO market raised a record HK$388 billion, representing a 106 percent year-on-year increase. Much of this capital flowed into AI, semiconductor and robotics companies.

Sin notes that Cyberport’s community has benefited directly from this favourable environment. “Between October 2025 and September 2026, Cyberport community enterprises secured HK$28.5 billion in funding, elevating total cumulative fundraising to over HK$74.5 billion. A substantial HK$20.8 billion of this total was driven by IPOs and strategic transactions.

Cyberport start-ups scale globally

Several Cyberport-supported companies exemplify this momentum. Cross-border fintech platform Qupital secured US$300 million following its Series C round, while data analytics platform Premialab raised US$220 million in funding. Global Web5 wealth technology platform Finloop also secured US$10 million after its A+ round.

For Qupital, Hong Kong and Cyberport have provided a crucial launchpad for international expansion.

“Our vision extends far beyond the local Hong Kong market as we set our sights firmly on the global stage. For our international expansion strategy, we have chosen the United States as our starting point, primarily due to its advanced AI ecosystem and massive e-commerce market. We are continually exploring avenues for broader worldwide growth,” says Winston Wong, co-founder and CEO of Qupital.

At CVCF 2026, the company will focus on building strategic relationships with investors and industry partners.

“Beyond venture capital and private equity firms, the event encompasses a vast array of portfolio companies, enabling us to easily identify potential partners with strong operational synergy,” Wong notes. “Our ultimate goal is to leverage the networks and technologies of these investors and their ecosystems to build enduring strategic partnerships that drive our long-term growth.”

Premialab likewise sees the forum as a valuable platform for growth. Co-founder and COO Pierre Trecourt believes its multi-stakeholder approach creates opportunities that extend well beyond fundraising.

“CVCF supports our strategic growth in three key areas. First, it helps attract top-tier talent and elevate the company's profile in Hong Kong. Second, it facilitates connections with venture capital and private equity investors who truly understand the business model and ecosystem. Finally, it drives joint R&D efforts with academic institutions, building on past successful collaborations with universities in Hong Kong and France to develop next-generation financial solutions.”

Founded at Cyberport in 2016, Premialab leveraged Hong Kong’s strong university talent pipeline and supportive innovation ecosystem before expanding into major international financial centres, Trecourt says. “This global presence enables Premialab to capture larger markets and collaborate closely with top-tier clients to continuously refine its solutions.”

From AI to the Agentic Economy

A major focus of CVCF 2026 will be the rise of agentic AI and its potential to transform business operations and financial services.

According to Zhao Yang, Deputy CEO of Finloop, the company is using agentic AI to identify emerging investment opportunities and automate complex workflows.

“We use it to analyse where capital is flowing. We have discovered instances where certain products perform exceptionally well, yet receive very little capital inflow, representing potential undervalued opportunities in the market,” Zhao notes. “We also handle processes like automated product screening. We have now integrated these tools into our proprietary platform, offering approximately ten specialised agentic AI solutions tailored for financial institutions. These are already successfully deployed with financial institutions today.”

CVCF 2026: where capital meets innovation

Beyond funding, CVCF 2026 explores how AI, Web3, tokenisation and cross-border capital flows are converging to reshape the global economy.

According to Eric Chan, Chief Public Mission Officer of Cyberport, the programme is designed to reflect this transformation. While the first day focuses on venture capital, innovation ecosystems and AI investment, the second day’s “Agentic Economy Summit” turns to enterprise and agentic AI, tokenisation, stablecoins and digital financial infrastructure. Together, the two days provide a forward-looking view of how technology and finance are evolving in parallel.

The event also highlights Hong Kong’s growing role as a gateway connecting capital, talent and innovation across Chinese Mainland, ASEAN, the Middle East and beyond.

Bringing together leading investors, founders, entrepreneurs, corporations, industry innovators and policymakers, CVCF 2026 will explore themes including enterprise and agentic AI, one-person companies (OPCs), frontier technologies and the future of digital finance. The forum will also showcase Hong Kong’s strategic position at the intersection of Chinese Mainland, ASEAN, the Middle East and global investment networks, while helping start-ups overcome financing and market-entry barriers to unlock new growth opportunities.

Complementing the conference programme, more than 50 exhibitors will showcase cutting-edge technology solutions, while dedicated one-on-one investor matching sessions will connect entrepreneurs and investors to explore partnerships, investments and business opportunities.

The Cyberport Venture & Capital Forum 2026

Venue: Cyberport

Date: November 4 and 5, 2026

title: Brazil’s study abroad ambitions widen, but information gap holds back demand
summary:
Growing interest in Europe, expanding bilingual schooling and demand for shorter overseas experiences are reshaping Brazil’s outbound student market, according to speakers preparing for The PIE High Brazil.

The post Brazil’s study abroad ambitions widen, but information gap holds back demand appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
While the US remains an important destination, Canada and Europe are seeing an undoubted rise in interest.

Speaking ahead of The PIE High Brazil, panellists described a market in which families are considering a wider range of countries and questioning assumptions about the cost – and ROI – of an international education.

But turning that interest into enrolments will require sustained engagement with schools and parents, they suggested, with new operators such as GlobalCamps helping high school students engage with the opportunity.

“There’s this conception that if you want to study abroad, it’s going to cost you USD $80,000 per year,” said Mauricio Segura of GlobalCamps, a platform connecting schools and their counsellors with summer and pre-university programS.

GlobalCamps works with approximately 150–200 schools across Brazil, according to Segura. Through school visits, fairs and parent sessions, he encounters students unfamiliar even with the possibility of taking a short university program during their school holidays.

“It’s a huge opportunity, but it’s a building block opportunity,” he said.

For universities seeking to recruit in Brazil, that means investing in market education alongside recruitment.

At Inspired’s Brazilian schools, Paulo Moraes described growing interest in students considering a degree overseas.

The group’s 12 schools in Brazil educate close to 8,000 pupils, although several are still developing their secondary provision. Across a current graduating cohort of around 250 students annually, Moraes estimated that approximately 15% choose to study abroad.

Most continue to university in Brazil, where families weigh competitive public university admissions against an increasingly attractive range of private institutions.

Among those looking overseas, Moraes said Europe and Canada now account for the majority of interest within his school network, contrasting with the stronger pull of the US seven or eight years ago.

Italy, Spain and Portugal feature prominently. For some families, dual citizenship makes European study particularly attractive financially.

“Many of our kids, they have a dual passport,” he said.

Isabel Baptista Zillig of Shorelight, which works with university partners predominantly in the US, reported a 60% increase in its Brazilian student numbers between 2025 and 2026.

She attributed that growth partly to explaining costs more clearly and providing reassurance about the support available once students arrive.

Across the universities Shorelight works with, Brazilian students paid average annual tuition of approximately US$19,000 in 2026, she said. Including living costs, insurance and meal plans, she put the annual total at around USD $35,000–40,000.

Those figures relate to Shorelight’s own students and university partners, but illustrate the gap speakers identified between perceptions of US study and the options available.

“Students, they don’t feel ready to go alone, to live without their families for the first time, and they need a lot of information and support,” said Baptista Zillig.

The expansion of bilingual schooling could help broaden the audience for those opportunities.

Thassiana Balbino Silva, business development manager for TOEFL iBT in Brazil, characterised the growth of bilingual programs over the past decade as preparation for a wider internationalisation of the school sector.

Balbino Silva also described Brazilian universities building international partnerships that allow students to spend part of their degree overseas. Baptista Zillig also reported growing interest in semester programs, including among students in fields such as law and medicine who intend to practise in Brazil.

For these students, shorter mobility can combine international experience with a domestic qualification and continued access to local professional networks.

Moraes said some families were increasingly conscious of the connections students might miss while completing an entire degree abroad.

Shorter experiences can address “both desires”, he suggested – gaining international exposure while building the relationships needed to start a career in Brazil.

Baptista Zillig stressed that overseas degrees bring their own networking advantages, particularly in destinations with strong commercial links to Brazil.

Together, the speakers’ observations point to an outbound market becoming more varied in both destination and format, with opportunities for providers able to explain the costs, support and career value of international study to a wider audience.

title: Foley Catheters and First-Year Composition: Implementing High-Impact Practices through Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration
summary:
