High Impact Practices (HIPs) use collaborative and active learning strategies to improve student engagements and outcomes. White (2018) explained that while HIPs can positively impact student success, budgetary restraints can present challenges to implementation. Therefore, […]

The post Foley Catheters and First-Year Composition: Implementing High-Impact Practices through Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
According to the Association of American Colleges and Universities, active learning is an essential part of a modern college education. High Impact Practices (HIPs) use collaborative and active learning strategies to improve student engagements and outcomes. White (2018) explained that while HIPs can positively impact student success, budgetary restraints can present challenges to implementation. Therefore, faculty are finding ways to create active learning experiences without a high cost to institutions.

Cross-disciplinary collaboration presents an opportunity to use HIPs to engage students in the core curriculum. In my case, the First-Year Writing (FYW) classroom offers a unique setting to use HIPs to build on how writing creates common spaces not only in FYW, but also expands those spaces into discipline-specific areas, such as nursing. Cross-disciplinary collaboration through FYW not only provides students with an early look at their majors but also teaches them how to decompartmentalize the writing skills they learn in FYW and apply them to a broader experience.

This article will focus on one such collaboration between English (English 1101) and Nursing and the impact of cross-disciplinary activities and HIPs on students in a discipline-specific FYW course.

Importance of Collaboration

Collaborative projects can provide students with deeper learning experiences and opportunities for increasing communication (written and oral) skills both inside the classroom and within the community (White, 2018; Bresciani, 2015). The FYW classroom provides a unique setting to build on momentum in cases where students are unable to have an early introduction to their major. FYW challenges students to understand the connection of strong writing to their majors, especially if the material in the course correlates to relevant subject matter in the major. The goal in creating this cost-effective nursing-specific English 1101 was to ask students to think specifically about how writing relates to a more universal experience (medical professions) in order to express the importance of humanities beyond the composition classroom.

Collaboration, particularly in course design and implementation, can often seem like a heavy lift. In some cases, faculty can be protective of course material and design, and in others, challenges exist in finding partnerships outside of specific disciplinary departments. In the following, I hope to show how this type of critical work can happen organically and effectively while bringing satisfaction and appreciation not only to students but to the faculty involved.

Process of Implementation

Over the course of a semester and over the summer, I worked with a nursing faculty member to refine the necessary concepts for bringing the course into the classroom. I started with the basic course learning outcomes for our institution’s English 1101.

From there, I and my nursing faculty partner, explored what concepts would be important for students interested in the nursing program to learn early in their academic careers. I began with highlighting the connection between the humanities and health care through learning about and constructing a medical narrative where students had to articulate their interest in pursuing a nursing career. Then, I focused on the importance of communication in relaying critical information through instructions by creating a process project, which included a demonstration (by my nursing partner) of a Foley catheter insertion using a medical mannequin, followed by a hands-on opportunity for students to practice this foundational healthcare procedure. Finally, I had students hone their research skills by exploring relevant and current healthcare-related issues and presenting them in a multimedia assignment. Instead of MLA, as is common in most humanities courses, students used APA formatting and citations throughout the course to better prepare them for the nursing program.

Please scan the QR code below for copies of the assignments.

Lessons Learned and Advice

Engagement

Students were more motivated to engage with assignments. They appreciated exposure to nursing concepts early in their academic careers and enjoyed forming an early relationship with a nursing faculty member. The course sparked their intellectual curiosity and got them thinking about the deeper issues within their major and future profession. When learning is decompartmentalized, students can see connection between academic and life experiences. Potential nursing students expressed excitement for discipline-specific core classes and, sometimes, students realized that the hands-on activities showed them that nursing was not their best fit, well before they spent years working towards acceptance into the nursing program.

Collaboration

Collaboration opportunities don’t have to be complicated, expensive, or overly time-consuming. Simple conversations and activities can be cost-effective while academically sound and engaging. Partnerships can happen in surprising situations. The nursing English 1101 collaboration started as a kernel of an idea while riding in the back of a college-issued Ford Taurus on the way home from a teaching and learning conference. It’s important to note that collaborative course work should involve immediate supervisors (chairs and deans), advisors, and the Registrar. In my situation, we needed to make sure the course was populated with future nursing students, which would be information the Registrar provided and advisors actively used for registration.

Final Thoughts

This collaboration provided students a way into a conversation about their major before they spent two years of preparation getting into their major courses. Unlike many other majors, nursing students do not take any nursing courses until they are accepted into the program, at least two years into their college education. For many, junior-level nursing courses are their first exposure to nursing concepts and conversations. A collaboration like the one I have presented allows an early look at disciplinary concepts and presents students with a stronger understanding of their educational decisions and career choices. Team teaching collaborative options and knowledge sharing that rely on HIPs, such as hands-on, experiential activities, can be designed to support strong communication skills and give students a concrete and vibrant support system that allows for intellectual curiosity and advanced critical thinking.

Dr. Stephanie B. Conner is a tenured associate professor of English with a focus on composition and Interdisciplinary Studies at the College of Coastal Georgia with over 25 years of experience. She has presented at nearly 40 conferences including the Conference on College Composition and Communication and published her work in journals such as Response to Writing. Her research is grounded in pedagogical best practices in college writing instruction as well as professional development in teaching and learning. Her most recent work includes a collaborative, dual-institution IRB-approved study with three other composition professors exploring faculty emotional responses to plagiarism and AI in writing courses and is due for publication at Composition Forum in spring 2026. Other research areas include incorporating Writing Center coaches into peer review activities and using weak examples as instructional material to bolster students’ critical thinking about citation and AI use. Dr. Conner has also worked collaboratively to develop a discipline-specific first-year writing course for students interested in the nursing program.

References

Bresciani, M. J. (2015). The neuroscience of learning and development and its implications for inquiry. Journal of Student Affairs Inquiry, 1(1), 1-11. https://vcsa.ucsd.edu/assessment/coalition/april-6_bresciani_the_neurosciene_of_learning_implications_for_inquiry.pdf

“High-Impact Practices | AAC&U.” American Association of Colleges and Universities, American Association of Colleges and Universities, https://www.aacu.org/trending-topics/high-impact. Accessed 6 Mar. 2026.

title: From Classroom to Career: An AI-Enhanced Scaffolded Job Interview Approach in the L2 Classroom
summary:
It is widely recognized among language instructors that effective second language teaching involves more than presenting grammar rules and vocabulary in isolation. Instead, meaningful learning develops when instructional activities connect to learners’ realities and lived experiences, enabling them to use the language to interpret, express, and negotiate meaning in contexts that matter to them. When […]

The post From Classroom to Career: An AI-Enhanced Scaffolded Job Interview Approach in the L2 Classroom appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
It is widely recognized among language instructors that effective second language teaching involves more than presenting grammar rules and vocabulary in isolation. Instead, meaningful learning develops when instructional activities connect to learners’ realities and lived experiences, enabling them to use the language to interpret, express, and negotiate meaning in contexts that matter to them. When classroom tasks reflect familiar situations—such as interacting in professional environments, navigating institutions, participating in multilingual communities, and communicating in person or through digital platforms—students engage more fully and demonstrate greater retention (Sujarwati, Iis et al.; Pérez-Núñez; Safarova). In these contexts, language functions not as an abstract object of study but as a communicative practice embedded in social life.

Building on this perspective, research in second language acquisition further shows that learning is strengthened when new linguistic knowledge is connected to prior experience (Vishnyakova et al.; Gajo; Müller; Mór). Learners interpret and retain language more effectively when forms are introduced through meaningful contexts that invite reflection, interaction, and purposeful expression. This understanding is so widely accepted in the field that the ACTFL World-Readiness Standards for Learning Languages reinforce it, emphasizing communication in real-world contexts and the development of intercultural competence. Together, these principles have shaped curricular design across proficiency levels, encouraging instructional practices that situate language within authentic communicative environments.

Within this broader pedagogical framework, textbooks and curricula often attempt to reflect learners’ daily lives by incorporating scenarios related to routines, social interactions, and academic experiences. As proficiency increases, students develop the linguistic range necessary to describe their perspectives with greater precision and complexity, engaging with disciplinary content such as literature, cultural analysis, or professional communication. However, despite this progression toward authenticity, one context that remains underutilized across the broader curriculum is the job interview (Calvo; Louw; Zekeri).

To address this gap, this article proposes the incorporation of job interview preparation and role-play activities beginning at the Spanish high-intermediate level and continuing into advanced courses, integrating reading, writing, and speaking within a communicative task that students perceive as both immediate and consequential. As learners approach graduation, their professional goals become more defined, and the need to articulate their experiences, strengths, and aspirations in the target language becomes increasingly relevant. In response, this article presents a scaffolded job interview activity designed to foster linguistic development, cultural reflection, and professional confidence across proficiency levels, allowing students to progressively refine their communicative strategies over time.

At the initial stage, students are introduced to core interview vocabulary and conventions through short video clips that illustrate a range of communicative styles. Selected excerpts from Spanish-language media, along with dubbed scenes from familiar television series—such as Betty la Fea and The Office (including hilarious Dwight’s job interviews in Spanish dubbing)—serve as accessible entry points for discussion. These materials function as conversational catalysts, encouraging students to analyze effective responses, identify common interview questions, and reflect on their own experiences. In classrooms characterized by diverse linguistic backgrounds and professional trajectories, these discussions often generate rich exchanges about expectations, challenges, and strategies for professional self-presentation.

As the activity progresses, students are introduced to structured approaches for responding to behavioral interview questions. One example is the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result), which provides a clear framework for organizing responses to prompts such as describing a professional challenge or explaining how a problem was resolved. Always in Spanish, Students analyze sample responses, examine how narrative structure contributes to clarity and persuasiveness, and begin constructing their own answers. At this stage, the focus extends beyond linguistic accuracy to rhetorical effectiveness, encouraging students to present their experiences in a coherent and compelling manner.

In addition, this stage prepares students to engage more critically and purposefully with ChatGPT in the following phase of the activity, which is completed as a guided homework assignment. In this simulation, students use artificial intelligence as both interviewer and language support tool, engaging in a structured practice interview outside the classroom. The instructions, originally written in Spanish, are provided below in translation for broader accessibility.

Guided Homework Activity: Job Interview Practice with ChatGPT

As part of this activity, the student will conduct a job interview in Spanish at home using ChatGPT. The goal is to strengthen speaking skills, expand vocabulary, and build confidence in professional communication before moving on to in-class role plays. Below are the instructions provided to the student.

Step 1: Choose a Position and Workplace

Select a job that interests you—your “dream job.” Be as specific as possible about both the position and the place where you would like to work (for example, the type of institution, organization, or company, and its location or context).

Step 2: Prepare Your Profile in Spanish

Write a short preparation note including:

The name of the position

A brief description of the job (2–3 sentences)

Three skills or experiences that make you a strong candidate

Information about the company or institution

Your professional and educational background

Step 3: Simulated Interview with ChatGPT

Copy and paste the following prompt into ChatGPT (you may adapt it to your chosen position):

“Act as an interviewer for a position as [job title] at [company, hospital, or institution]. The interview will be conducted in Spanish. Ask me between 5 and 7 typical job interview questions for this position. After each of my responses, provide brief corrections or comments on how I can improve my expression, grammar, or vocabulary. Use a formal tone, as in a real job interview.”

During the simulation:

Respond orally to each question (you may use the microphone feature to record your answers).

Respond as naturally as possible, as if in a real interview.

Carefully review the feedback provided by ChatGPT after each response.

Use the suggestions to refine subsequent answers.

Save useful feedback for future reference.

At the end, save the full transcript of your interview, including both responses and feedback.

After the simulation:

Review your responses and ChatGPT’s feedback carefully.

Write a revised version of your answers, incorporating improvements where appropriate.

Read your revised responses aloud to practice pronunciation and fluency.

Be prepared to share insights and key takeaways in our in-class discussion.

Classroom Implementation and Student Impact

This is the fourth semester in which I have incorporated a ChatGPT-based component into a job interview activity that I have developed and refined over several years. Student feedback has been consistently positive, particularly regarding the value of AI-generated feedback in helping them refine their responses and develop more precise, context-appropriate vocabulary. Many students also note that practicing in a lower-anxiety, interactive environment increases their confidence, especially when they later participate in in-class role plays where they alternate roles as interviewer and candidate.

In the third segment of the activity, students first work in pairs in the classroom and then continue collaborating outside of class over the course of a week as they prepare for a final in-class simulation: a “grand finale” interview in which they apply for a position aligned with their professional aspirations. After each performance, classmates identify strengths and effective strategies demonstrated by their peers, while suggestions for improvement are offered in general terms to support collective reflection and ongoing learning at the end of all presentations.

As mentioned earlier, I typically implement this activity first in high-intermediate Spanish courses and then revisit it in advanced-level courses. This progression across semesters reveals noticeable gains in fluency, confidence, and professional discourse. In advanced courses, it is not uncommon for students to be actively applying for real positions while completing the activity. Many report feeling significantly more comfortable articulating their skills, experiences, and goals in interview settings, often noting that the transfer from Spanish to English interview contexts feels unexpectedly seamless.

Although the controlled classroom environment cannot fully replicate the unpredictability of real interviews, many of the most common questions—such as describing oneself, discussing experience, articulating strengths and weaknesses, explaining motivation, or imagining future goals—remain consistent across contexts. Because students recognize the direct relevance of these tasks, engagement increases substantially. As one student remarked, this is “useful stuff,” a comment that captures the pedagogical value of aligning language learning with authentic communicative needs. My experience in the classroom has also been echoed in the work of other instructors who have implemented similar activities in different disciplinary contexts. Calvo-Benzies (2021) in the field of tourism, notes that learners often “crave” the practical application offered by job interview simulations, as these tasks provide a tangible sense of reality while developing transferable professional skills that extend beyond the classroom. Such findings reinforce the relevance and longevity of this type of instructional design.

For this reason, repeating the job interview activity across consecutive courses creates an additional layer of development, allowing students not only to improve but also to recognize their own progress over time. This visible trajectory of growth strengthens confidence, reinforces motivation, and deepens students’ sense of agency as multilingual speakers capable of navigating real-world professional spaces in more than one language.

Ultimately, we as faculty are part of the growth and development not only of our subject of expertise but also of well-rounded human beings whom we hope to support and see succeed. Teaching language, in this sense, is teaching for life itself: it is about the joys of what students will go on to accomplish, the confidence they will carry forward, and the meaningful ways they will use their voices in the world beyond the classroom.

Angela Rodriguez Mooney, PhD, is an assistant professor of Spanish at Texas Woman’s University.

References

American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages. World-Readiness Standards for Learning Languages: The Roadmap to Language Competence. ACTFL, https://www.actfl.org/educator-resources/world-readiness-standards-for-learning-languages. Accessed 10 Apr. 2026.

Calvo Benzies, Yolanda Joy. “Levelling Up the English for Tourism (EFT) Classroom with Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools: Practical Contributions for Preparing and Succeeding at Job Interviews.” Revolucionando la docencia universitaria: innovación educativa en la era de la IA y la gamificación, edited by Teresa Barceló Ugarte, Alejandro Martín García, and Manuel Mora Márquez, Dykinson, 2024, pp. 301–334.

—. “Bringing Authentic Materials into the ESP Classroom to Enhance Oral Skills: A Case Study on Tourism Students’ Attitudes towards a Simulated Job Interview.” Fifth International Conference on Foreign Languages and Tourism, 12–13 Nov. 2021.

Gajo, Laurent. “Linguistic Knowledge and Subject Knowledge: How Does Bilingualism Contribute to Subject Development?” International Journal of Bilingual Education and Bilingualism, vol. 10, no. 5, 2007, pp. 563–581.

Louw, Kerry J., et al. “Teaching Pragmatics to L2 Learners for the Workplace: The Job Interview.” The Canadian Modern Language Review / La revue canadienne des langues vivantes, vol. 66, no. 5, 2010, pp. 739–758.

Mór, Walkyria Monte. “Learning by Design: Reconstructing Knowledge Processes in Teaching and Learning Practices.” A Pedagogy of Multiliteracies: Learning by Design, Palgrave Macmillan UK, 2015, pp. 186–209.

Müller, Terry. “Prior Learning Narrative: Facilitating Reflection to Connect Experience to Learning.” The Journal of Continuing Higher Education, vol. 60, no. 3, 2012, pp. 181–185.

Pérez-Núñez, Antonio. “Mobile-Enhanced Virtual Exchanges through Asynchronous Video Interaction: Learners as Ethnographers in the L2 Classroom to Promote Intercultural Communicative Competence.” Journal of Virtual Exchange, 2024.

Safarova, N. “Interactive Approaches in Spanish Language Acquisition: Expanding Educational Horizons for University Students.” UNIVERSUM, 20–24.

Sujarwati, Iis, et al. “Exploring Vocabulary Retention and Student Engagement: A Dive into Gamified vs. Traditional Flipped Classroom.” JEELS (Journal of English Education and Linguistics Studies), 2025.

Texas Woman’s University Career Connections. “The STAR Method.” Career Connections, Texas Woman’s University, https://careerconnections.twu.edu/resources/the-star-method/. Accessed 10 Apr. 2026.

Vishnyakova, Olga D., Elena S. Markova, and Timofey V. Leonov. “The Role of Prior Knowledge in Formative Assessment for Linguistic Competence Development.” Professional Discourse & Communication, vol. 5, no. 4, 2023, pp. 68–78.

Zekeri, Andrew A. “College curriculum competencies and skills former students found essential to their careers.” College Student Journal, vol. 38, no. 3, Sept. 2004, pp. 412-423.

title: We Investigated: Pennsylvania’s Most Elite Colleges
summary: College Library Study “Elite” here refers to academic distinction rather than equally selective admissions. Pennsylvania is home to a range of higher education options, from large research universities to colleges combining engineering and liberal arts, or schools built around a demanding senior thesis. These schools differ in size and focus. For this list, we gave […]
full_text:
“Elite” here refers to academic distinction rather than equally selective admissions.

Pennsylvania is home to a range of higher education options, from large research universities to colleges combining engineering and liberal arts, or schools built around a demanding senior thesis. These schools differ in size and focus. For this list, we gave the most weight to documented academic distinction, followed by research opportunities, undergraduate engagement, and impact beyond a narrow local mission.

That means broad research universities have an advantage near the top, while smaller schools still earned credit for focused educational strengths. This list isn’t a ranking by selectivity, and it isn’t an official ranking.

Use it as a starting point to compare programs, support, learning expectations, and cost, and judge the fit.

15

Gettysburg College

Connects Liberal Arts Study With Practice

Gettysburg College is a small college in Pennsylvania that emphasizes undergraduate education and teaching alongside research.1

Its undergraduate programs emphasize theory and practice, giving students many opportunities to apply what they’ve learned.2 Students considering Gettysburg can explore the flexibility of studying the liberal arts and sciences at a small college. The college’s approach supports close relationships between students and professors, and can help students gain practical experience applying the theories they’re learning in class.2

Prospective students should explore projects involving students and faculty members in the programs that interest them. They should also examine the support systems available.

Students who connect classes and experiences can leave with stronger thinking and research skills, a greater sense of purpose in their studies, and preparation for further study or work.

Students looking for a well-rounded liberal arts education that doesn’t pigeonhole them into one specialty may thrive in Gettysburg’s programs.

14

Dickinson College

Links Global Learning With Sustainability

Global learning is at Dickinson’s core.

Sustainability runs through many aspects of life at Dickinson, from courses and research projects to facilities management and community involvement.4 Students interested in furthering their understanding of sustainability issues through field-based experiences can explore opportunities. Students in other disciplines can explore ways that sustainability intersects with their areas of study.

Its approach to global education encourages students to step outside the classroom and investigate complicated issues by gathering and assessing evidence. Students draw on insights from multiple fields of study and make informed decisions.

Faculty collaboration and student research projects reflect Dickinson’s dedication to linking academic learning with real-world problems.3 Dickinson’s resources, such as its organic farm, offer connections between theory and practice.4

If global learning or sustainability aren’t your primary academic interests, you can still appreciate these components of the Dickinson experience and understand their relevance to your area of study.

13

Drexel University

Integrates Professional Work Into Degree Study

Drexel University’s cooperative education program is central to its academic model.5 The applied learning opportunities are integrated throughout the academic program, with learning guided by industry professionals and Drexel faculty.6

Cooperative education at Drexel is hands-on professional work experience that’s related to a student’s academic and career objectives. In a co-op position, students work on real projects with deliverables and deadlines.

This type of experience benefits from preparation and connections back to the student’s degree program. Drexel’s research university setting supports its cooperative education model. Drexel combines cooperative education with a rigorous academic curriculum, giving students experience alongside their studies.

Prospective students should understand how cooperative education works within their particular degree program, including when co-ops take place, how positions are acquired and how they fit into the curriculum.

Check which expenses continue during each part of the degree.

12

Franklin & Marshall College

Offers Faculty-Mentored Research Across Fields

Franklin & Marshall College encourages hands-on research with faculty mentors.7 The college offers a Summer Research Scholars program in which students work with faculty mentors in the sciences, the social sciences, the humanities and the arts.8 Having a summer research program does not mean there will be a position for every student.

At Franklin & Marshall, research is not just for science students, and it does not just take place in the lab. Experiential learning is an important part of the F&M experience, and can take place in museums, studios, in the community, and more. Experiential learning can be a way to try out different areas of study and find your niche before narrowing your academic focus.

Students should find out how people in their area of interest join research projects, and what assistance is available.

Franklin & Marshall makes a clear distinction between research projects that are part of a particular course and those that students pursue on their own.8 Students should ask about the balance of the two at F&M.

Research experiences can help students gain a deeper understanding of a field of study and can produce a substantial project. There’s also the experience of fielding criticism about your original work.

11

The University of Pittsburgh

Connects Broad Study With Faculty Research

The University of Pittsburgh offers students access to a major research environment. Pitt is a public, research-focused school and a member of the Association of American Universities.9

Pitt offers students opportunities to connect their classroom learning to hands-on experience, work alongside faculty members, and get involved in research projects.10

As at many research-focused institutions, Pitt students who want to get involved in research at an early stage may benefit from narrowing their research interests and choosing a manageable scope.

Pitt’s undergraduate advising system can help with this. Advising approaches vary by college or school, so compare the support available.

To judge the fit, compare what Pitt offers within your intended program of study with other schools.

10

Penn State University Park

Combines Academic Range With Research Support

This entry covers Penn State’s University Park campus.11 Beyond its size, Penn State’s academic range and campus community may appeal.

Prospective students should check where each Penn State program starts and ends. Students sometimes start at one campus and complete their degree at University Park. Check the requirements for changing campuses and whether the pathway suits your situation.

Students can also benefit from Penn State’s undergraduate research resources.

Penn State research ambassadors and staff can help students find research that interests them and connect with faculty mentors.12 Finding research opportunities and a mentor isn’t always straightforward.

9

Villanova University

Grounds Its Learning Goals in Augustinian Values

Villanova’s learning goals emphasize knowledge in a specific academic discipline, alongside broader skills, such as effective communication and an appreciation for diverse cultures.13

Villanova’s goals integrate the university’s Catholic, Augustinian philosophical heritage.13 They envision a college education that is more than preparation for a career.

Its place within the Catholic intellectual tradition is expressed in its theology and religion requirement.14 This also encourages students to approach religion from historical, cultural and disciplinary perspectives.

If Villanova appeals to you, consider whether its aims align with your educational goals.

Villanova articulates the aims of an education, and of the personal qualities such an education should help develop. Some of Villanova’s undergraduate schools and colleges may have requirements that supplement these university-wide goals. Check the specific requirements of your intended college or school.

8

Bucknell University

Combines Liberal Arts, Engineering, and Management

Engineering, management, and the liberal arts are all represented in their own colleges, giving the university academic breadth.15

Students can combine academic interests across subjects.16 Maybe you want to apply management strategies to solve engineering problems, or explore a scientific issue relevant to the business world.

Students considering Bucknell should plan carefully when mapping out their course of study. Prospective students should check which college their intended major resides in. More structured programs, like engineering, may limit a student’s ability to explore other subjects.

A suitable course of study might be one that weaves multiple subjects together, while leaving time for your primary interest and room for a secondary one.

7

Lafayette College

Combines Undergraduate Liberal Arts With Engineering

Lafayette College earns its place here for opportunities for undergraduates to research with faculty, pursue independent studies or complete honors theses.18 Lafayette doesn’t award graduate degrees.17

Lafayette’s undergraduate engineering and liberal arts programs benefit from each other because the school focuses on undergraduates. Its resources, from science and technical facilities to arts centers and research libraries, support students seeking their first degree. Lafayette’s engineering students also benefit from its liberal arts core curriculum that combines a common course of study with a first-year seminar.

Engineering and science students can seek positions as paid research assistants working alongside faculty members and pursue honors theses.18

Students interested in Lafayette should check that degree requirements allow them to pursue both parts of their academic interests. Applicants should also ask how undergraduates join research, including how they find a mentor.

6

Bryn Mawr College

Pairs Undergraduate Study With Original Research

Bryn Mawr is a residential liberal arts college for women. It offers undergraduate education in the sciences, social sciences, humanities, and arts, alongside graduate programs and research.19

Bryn Mawr’s close collaboration with Haverford College expands its students’ academic options.20 Here, an emphasis on primary reading and research, experimentation, and dialogue supports original undergraduate scholarship.20

Prospective students should examine individual departments and programs, noting whether they’re graduate or undergraduate offerings.

Check that cross-registration opportunities fulfill your degree requirements. Browse some student work to get a sense of the academic culture. Prestige means different things to different people, but at Bryn Mawr it can mean developing as a scholar in a chosen field.

5

Lehigh University

Offers Degrees That Combine Business, Engineering, Health, and Arts

Lehigh University emphasizes research, faculty mentorship and collaborative efforts that extend beyond campus life.21

Students can pursue interdisciplinary programs at Lehigh that cross boundaries among its schools and departments, including in the arts, business, computing, engineering, and health fields.22

Lehigh’s interdisciplinary programs are structured. Applicants should examine the requirements and admissions processes for each track. While these interdisciplinary options may suit applicants with a variety of interests, each option requires planning.

Students should compare the research opportunities available in their intended fields and consider how to combine different approaches. The goal is a coherent educational experience.

4

Haverford College

Requires Every Student to Complete a Senior Thesis

Every Haverford student completes a senior thesis, an original project in which students are mentored by faculty and learn about and contribute to research in their field of study.23

Haverford’s Honor Code stresses the importance of academic integrity, self-direction, and respect for knowledge.24

Ranked fourth on our list, Haverford College offers a rigorous educational experience that’s built on research, integrity, and intellectual exploration. The Honor Code and the senior thesis requirement highlight the College’s dedication to research and its emphasis on personal responsibility and academic excellence.

Students looking to apply to Haverford should browse the senior thesis projects in their field of interest. Their work can show the commitment and scholarship that Haverford expects.

If this work appeals to you and you want a community that emphasizes integrity and research, Haverford College may suit you.

3

Swarthmore College

Tests Honors Students Through Outside Examiners

Swarthmore’s Honors Program provides students with a rigorous academic experience that culminates in written and oral exams administered by outside experts.25 Swarthmore students interested in the Honors Program should be prepared for specialized seminars, one-on-one and small-group work with faculty, special projects, and outside exams.25

Students who excel at defending and discussing their coursework may want to consider applying to the Honors Program. Those who prefer other assessments may want to consider alternatives. The program adds depth to Swarthmore’s undergraduate education.

Swarthmore offers a Bachelor of Arts or, in engineering, a Bachelor of Science.26

2

Carnegie Mellon University

Connects Technical and Creative Fields

Carnegie Mellon University isn’t only focused on computing, engineering, and other traditionally technical fields. It has programs in a variety of fields, including brain and cognitive science and the arts.27

CMU values interdisciplinarity.

Its undergraduate and research programs recognize that many problems need more than one perspective.28 The intersection of disciplines can inspire CMU students, from examining design issues in technical systems to exploring how computation and new technologies can support creative pursuits. We reward this commitment to forging connections in our rankings.

CMU comprises several schools and colleges, each with its own admissions requirements. Check the admissions criteria for your intended program.

While CMU encourages interdisciplinary exploration, restrictions can apply to transferring into an interdisciplinary program.

If you are interested in combining technical and creative work, CMU may appeal.

1

The University of Pennsylvania

Leads Our List for Breadth and Undergraduate Scholarship

This is the University of Pennsylvania, distinct from Penn State.

For breadth and structured undergraduate scholarship, Penn earns our top spot. This is an editorial judgment, not a claim that Penn ranks first for every student or every field of study.

Penn’s undergraduate students study in one of four undergraduate schools.29 These provide breadth and an intellectual home base within a large graduate and professional institution.

Through the Center for Undergraduate Research and Fellowships, students can find focused research communities, connect with like-minded scholars through seminars, or pursue independent research projects with the support of a faculty mentor.30

Each opportunity has its own application and participation requirements. Together, these resources provide undergrads with defined paths toward advanced scholarship at Penn. Penn’s programs can provide breadth through research opportunities and connections, or depth through research projects with faculty mentors.30

The school you’ll apply to, the realistic opportunities you’ll have once there, and the cost after aid are all important to consider. Prestige matters less than knowing your goals and understanding how Penn’s resources can help.

full_text:
Westermann, Anja; Neiske, Iris (2026): KI-Kompetenz: Orientierung und Praxis für Studierende – Konzeption eines modularen Moodle-Selbstlernkurses. In: Mayer, Frank; Czech, Henning; Sieg, Julia; Ehnert, Sabine (Hrsg.): Persönlichkeit trifft Didaktik: Lernräume für eine Welt im Wandel. Schriftenreihe „Voneinander Lehren lernen“, S. 118-123. DOI: https://doi.org/10.48769/opus-9142

In der Schriftenreihe „Voneinander Lehren lernen“ werden an der Hochschule Osnabrück anwendungsbezogene Beiträge zur Qualitätsentwicklung in Studium und Lehre publiziert. Die Schriftenreihe ist an das Konzept des „Scholarship of Teaching and Learning“ (SoTL) angelehnt. Demnach soll sie den Lehrenden verschiedener Studiengänge als Plattform dienen, um ihre eigenen Erfahrungen, Ideen und Konzepte zur Lehr- und Studiengangentwicklung systematisch zu reflektieren und entsprechende Erkenntnisse für andere nutzbar zu machen. Ziel ist es, den Diskurs über hochschuldidaktische Themen in die Fächer zu tragen und so die Qualität der Lehr-Lernprozesse in den Studiengängen zu fördern.

Dieser sechste Band ist eine Dokumentation zur Veranstaltung „Persönlichkeit trifft Didaktik: Lernräume für eine Welt im Wandel“, die am 04. und 05. Dezember 2025 an der Hochschule Osnabrück stattgefunden hat. Unter dem Motto „Lehr-Lernkonferenz meets ICM & beyond“ wurde die üblicherweise hochschulinterne Lehr-Lernkonferenz für externe Teilnehmende geöffnet und gemeinsam mit der 14. Konferenz des Netzwerks „Inverted Classroom & beyond“ ausgerichtet.

Ausgehend von den Workshops, Vorträgen und Postern auf der Veranstaltung entstand eine vielfältige Sammlung von Texten, die zu drei inhaltlichen Clustern arrangiert wurden: Im ersten Teil stehen Rollen und Haltungen sowie damit verbundene didaktische Entscheidungen von Lehrenden im Fokus. Der zweite Teil richtet den Blick auf Begegnung, Zusammenarbeit und Chancengerechtigkeit innerhalb von Lehr-Lern-Gemeinschaften. Individualisierung und studentische Persönlichkeitsentwicklung sowie ihre Unterstützung durch Technologien bilden den Schwerpunkt des dritten Teils. Mehr informationen unter: https://opus.bsz-bw.de/hsos/frontdoor/index/index/docId/9142
